title: Contend for the Faith; Kept by the God Who Is Able
summary: Jude urges his readers to contend for the faith once entrusted to the saints, because ungodly people have slipped into the church, turning grace into license and denying Jesus Christ. He recalls God's judgments on the wilderness generation, the angels who left their place, and Sodom and Gomorrah, and he describes the intruders with images drawn from Scripture, tradition, and nature, including a prophecy of Enoch. He then calls the faithful to build themselves up, pray, keep themselves in God's love, and show mercy, and closes with praise to the God who is able to keep them from stumbling.
story: Jude is a single-chapter letter written in the generation after Jesus, when the church already had a faith to hand down and people inside it willing to twist it. It gathers Israel's history, from Cain to the exodus and Balaam, as warning for the present. Its closest neighbor is 2 Peter 2, which contains much of the same material. It stands just before Revelation, and its closing looks forward to the day when Christ's people are presented blameless before God's glory with great joy.
historical:
The writer is Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James. The James needing no further description is almost certainly James the brother of Jesus and leader of the Jerusalem church, which makes Jude also a brother of Jesus (Mark 6:3 lists a Judas among them). Like James, he did not believe in Jesus during his ministry (John 7:5) but came to faith afterward. The early church historian Eusebius, quoting the second-century writer Hegesippus, tells of Jude's grandsons, working farmers, who were questioned by the emperor Domitian about their descent from David and released. Some scholars regard the letter as pseudonymous, written later in Jude's name; others accept it as his, and date it between about AD 50 and 80.

Jude makes use of two traditions outside the Old Testament. Verses 14-15 quote a prophecy attributed to Enoch that closely matches 1 Enoch 1:9, part of a collection of Jewish writings composed over the last centuries before Christ; Aramaic fragments of it were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. Verse 9 refers to a dispute between the archangel Michael and the devil over the body of Moses. Early Christian writers, including Origen, said this story came from a work called the Assumption of Moses. A related text, known as the Testament of Moses, survives in part, but its ending is lost, so the passage Jude drew on cannot be checked directly.
cultural:
The intruders took part in the church's love feasts (verse 12), the shared meals at which early Christians ate together, the rich supplying the poor, often with the Lord's Supper. Jude calls the intruders hidden reefs there, or possibly stains; the Greek word spilas usually meant a rock hidden under the water, a danger to ships. His images come quickly: clouds that promise rain but give none, trees without fruit even in harvest season, waves casting up foam, stars wandering off course. Ancient sailors and travelers steered by the stars, and a wandering star (probably a planet or meteor) was of no use as a guide.

Jewish readers of Jude's day knew a large body of tradition that retold and expanded the Scriptures. The angels who left their proper dwelling (verse 6) recall Genesis 6:1-4 as it was read in 1 Enoch, where heavenly watchers took human wives and were imprisoned in darkness until judgment. Cain, Balaam, and Korah (verse 11) had become stock examples of envy, greed, and rebellion. Jude's readers would have caught the allusions immediately, and he assumes they know the stories well (verse 5).
literary: Jude is carefully structured and fond of threes. His readers are called, loved, and kept (verse 1); he wishes them mercy, peace, and love (verse 2). He gives three examples of judgment (verses 5-7), three charges against the intruders (verse 8), three Old Testament figures (verse 11), and three groups to show mercy to (verses 22-23). The central section alternates between examples from Scripture and tradition and the phrase these men (verses 8, 10, 12, 16, 19), applying each example to the intruders. The letter is framed by keeping: those kept in Jesus Christ (verse 1), keep yourselves in the love of God (verse 21), and the God who is able to keep you from stumbling (verse 24). The doxology of verses 24-25 is one of the most beautiful in the New Testament.

outline.t: Greeting to the called, loved, and kept
Contend for the faith against those who slipped in
The intruders: slanderers, Cain, Balaam, Korah
Remember, build, keep, and show mercy
Doxology to the God who keeps

doctrines.note: The faith was entrusted once for all to the saints (verse 3). It is a received deposit, not an evolving opinion, and the church guards it rather than revising it.
God judged unbelief in the wilderness, rebellion among the angels, and immorality at Sodom. Jude uses these to warn that the church is not exempt, and that the Lord will come to judge the ungodly.
Believers are kept in Jesus Christ and await his mercy that brings eternal life. The God who called them is able to keep them from stumbling and present them blameless with great joy.
Praying in the Holy Spirit is one of the ways believers build themselves up and keep themselves in God's love (verses 20-21). Prayer is a defense, not only a devotion.

words.note: Epagonizomai, to contend or fight earnestly, from the word for an athletic contest or struggle. It appears only here in the New Testament. Jude calls believers to strive for the faith, not with violence, but with the determination of an athlete in competition.

Spilas, a hidden reef, a rock under the surface that wrecks ships. Some translate it as spots or stains, from a similar word used in 2 Peter 2:13. Either way, the intruders are a hidden danger at the heart of the church's fellowship meal.

Tereo, to keep, guard, or protect. It frames the letter: believers are kept in (or for) Jesus Christ (verse 1), rebellious angels are kept in chains (verse 6), darkness is kept for the ungodly (verse 13), and believers must keep themselves in God's love (verse 21). The God who keeps and the believer who keeps stand side by side.

christ: Jude calls Jesus Christ our only Master and Lord (verse 4), using a word for master (despotes) often applied to God. In verse 5, the BSB follows several early manuscripts in saying that Jesus delivered his people out of Egypt; other manuscripts read the Lord or God. If Jesus is the original reading, Jude identifies Christ with the God who acted in Israel's history. Believers are kept in Jesus Christ (verse 1), await his mercy leading to eternal life (verse 21), and give glory to God through Jesus Christ our Lord (verse 25). The Lord who is coming with his holy ones to judge (verse 14) is, in early Christian reading, Christ himself.

hard.q: Why does Jude quote 1 Enoch and a tradition about Moses, and does that make those books Scripture?
hard.a:
Jude plainly quotes a prophecy that matches 1 Enoch 1:9 and draws on a story about Michael and the body of Moses that is not in the Old Testament. This troubled some in the early church; Jerome, in the late fourth century, noted that many rejected the letter for that reason. Others, including Tertullian, argued that Jude's use of Enoch showed the book had value.

Christians have generally responded in one of several ways. Some say that quoting a book is not the same as endorsing it as a whole; Paul quotes Greek poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12) and a Jewish tradition about Jannes and Jambres (2 Timothy 3:8) without treating those sources as Scripture. On this view, Jude affirms that this particular saying is a true prophecy about the Lord's coming, which agrees with Old Testament teaching, without canonizing the rest of 1 Enoch. Others note that Jude was writing to readers who valued these works and used them as common ground. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church, by contrast, includes 1 Enoch in its Bible. For most churches, Jude's use of the tradition shows how deeply the first Christians lived in the Jewish world of their day, and how the Spirit could use that world to speak.

questions: Jude intended to write about shared salvation but felt he had to urge his readers to contend for the faith. When is it right to shift from encouragement to warning?
The intruders turned grace into license. In what ways can grace be misused today to excuse what God calls sin?
Jude ends by calling the faithful to show mercy to those who doubt and to snatch others from the fire. How do you hold firm conviction and tender mercy together?
